transcript.text: I am the product manager for the checkout of an online furniture shop. We tested a new one-page checkout against the old three-step one. The test was planned for four weeks, but I looked at the results every morning, and on day nine the new page was ahead: 3.4 percent of visitors bought against 3.0 percent, and our testing tool showed a 95 percent chance that the new page is better, so I stopped the test. About 11,000 visitors saw each version. The average order value was a little lower on the new page. Returning customers seemed to like it less and new visitors more. The developers want to remove the old checkout this week. I have only the summary screen of the testing tool, no export. I make the call. Should we ship it?

My answer: no — don't ship permanently this week, and above all don't let the developers delete the old checkout. The evidence is real but weaker than the "95%" makes it look, and the risk here is not the page, it is the point of no return.

Four things drive that. First, you looked nine mornings and stopped at the first good one. A tool that fires "95% likely better" each morning will show you that number at some point in nine days on a genuinely flat test roughly one time in five, so the honest reading of 3.4% against 3.0% at 11,000 visitors each is "promising, not proven" — on a single planned look that gap sits just outside the usual significance line. Second, your four-week plan was right: to detect a lift of this size reliably you need something like three times the traffic you had on day 9, so you stopped with about a third of the evidence. Third, purchase rate is the wrong finish line for furniture. Fourth, returning customers liking it less is a warning, not noise: they are usually your highest-intent, highest-basket slice, and a flat overall number can hide a real loss there. Day 9 is also inside the novelty window, where new-visitor gains look best and returning-customer resistance is at its worst.

The plan:

1. This week, keep both code paths. Freeze the deletion. It costs nothing and keeps every later option open.
2. Don't choose between "ship" and "don't".
3. Fix the measure before you look again: revenue per visitor, plus the same split for new and returning visitors.
4. Get the raw numbers out of the tool even by hand — per-arm conversions, AOV, and the new-versus-returning counts. If they can't be extracted, that is itself a finding about your testing setup.
5. Ship permanently only if revenue per visitor is ahead at the planned end and returning-customer revenue is not meaningfully down.

If you can get me the per-arm AOV and the new-versus-returning visitor counts, I can work out revenue per visitor and whether the returning-customer drop is large enough to change the call.

I want a recommendation engine like the big sites have: when a customer logs in, the app shows the destination they are most likely to book next. The table I shared is our booking export: one row per booking with a booking id, the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, whether it was cancelled, and the customer id. We sell five destinations. The app team will put one destination at the top of the home screen for each logged-in customer. Please build it. [shares bookings.csv]

Understood: for every logged-in customer the app shows one of your five destinations at the top, and you want the engine that picks it. I've started the prediction project (outcome: `destination`). What the export shows, and what it changes. The real question behind your brief isn't "which destination", it's "which answer can I trust per customer": most months book just above the number of distinct customers (January 2026: 113 bookings, 108 customers), so a customer's own history is thin and a lot of login traffic will have no prior booking. That's why I'd not train a plain "predict this booking's destination" model: its own price, free_cancellation, cancelled, lead time and travel date describe the answer and would leak it. Score with a time split — train on earlier bookings, test on the latest months, never a random shuffle, so the number is what the app would see live. 3. Measure top-1 accuracy against the "most popular destination" baseline and against "the destination they booked last time". 4. Stop rule: if the model doesn't beat both baselines, you get the best simple rule instead of a model, plus the per-nationality and per-channel rankings the app team can ship. 5. Deliver a ranked destination per customer id, with a note on which customers are cold-start. DCLab is checking the remaining build requirements now.

transcript.text: I lead customer experience at a subscription company. The chief executive asked me why customers leave. Please build a model on the table I shared and give me the top three reasons, ranked, so the product team can fix them next quarter. The table has one row per customer: customer id, signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. I will present the three reasons to the management team, and the product roadmap for the quarter will follow them. [shares customers.csv]

Built it. Here's what I understood and what happens next. **Your problem isn't "why do customers leave" in general — it's which three things the product team can change next quarter.** That distinction matters, because a model ranks what predicts churn, and not everything that predicts is something you can fix (tenure, for example, predicts strongly but isn't a roadmap item). So I'll separate drivers into "actionable" and "just descriptive" when the numbers come back. What your table already tells me: 1,200 customers, 17.4% churned the next month. Consumer churns at 18.1% (961 customers) versus business at 14.6% (239) — a real gap, though the business group is the smaller of the two. I'm reading `churned_next_month` as the label and `support_tickets_90d` as recent support load; tell me if either is wrong. The plan:

1. **Train on a held-out slice, not the whole table.** Churn has a date attached, so the model scores customers it never saw, the way it would next quarter. Checked by accuracy on that holdout versus the base rate of 17.4%. 2. **Rank the drivers.** Which features move churn probability most, with size and direction — so "tickets up" comes with "churn goes from X% to Y%". 3. **Filter to what the product team controls.** Plan, support load, spend, signup cohort. Segment and city get reported as context, not as reasons. 4. **Flag the one trap.** Tickets in the last 90 days partly overlap the month churn happens, so a ticket can be a symptom of someone already leaving. I'll say which way each driver most plausibly runs rather than let the deck imply cause. 5. **Give you three, ranked, each with the number of customers it covers** — so the roadmap has an owner and a size, not just a label. DCLab is checking the remaining build requirements now; I'll bring the ranked drivers back as soon as it has run.

transcript.text: I am the expansion manager of a bakery and café chain with 14 shops, all in Dubai and Sharjah. In three months we open our first shop in Riyadh. My finance director wants a machine learning forecast of the new shop's daily sales for its first six months. We need it to fix the staff roster, to decide whether to buy two ovens or three, and to sign the first flour contract. We have three years of daily sales for every shop and product, and each shop's size, rent and opening date. Nothing is exported yet. We have never run a shop outside the UAE. The lease is signed, so the opening itself is not in question. What would you do?

Understood: this isn't one forecast, it's three decisions wearing the costume of one. The roster needs the day-by-day shape (which days, which hours); the ovens need the busiest day, not the average; the flour contract needs cumulative ingredient volume. A single average daily line is the wrong deliverable — it leaves the kitchen short on the peak and the roster wrong on the quiet day.

The harder truth: your data has never seen Riyadh. A model trained on your 14 shops cannot invent a Saudi demand level, and the weekly pattern will shift, since the working week and the weekend are not the same there. What a model *can* do well is learn from the shops you've already opened what the first six months of a new bakery of yours look like — the ramp to steady state, the day-of-week shape, the bakery-versus-café mix. The *level* has to come from your judgement: which shop is the closest match by size and format, or a sales-per-square-metre target. I'd rather build that in openly than hide it behind a decimal point.

The plan:
1. Export daily sales by shop and product with size, rent and opening date into one table; I check the columns and any shop with too short a history.
2. Measure the ramp and the weekly shape from your own launches, and flag where a Riyadh week will differ.
3. Validate before you trust it: hold out your two newest shops, forecast them as if they were new, compare with what actually happened. If the error is too large, you know cheaply and we stop.
4. Apply it to Riyadh at the level you name, as a low, middle and high daily line.

transcript.text: I am the head of customer service at a home internet provider with about 80,000 customers. Last month we emailed a satisfaction survey to all of them and 4,900 answered. Of those, 71 percent said they are satisfied or very satisfied. People who had contacted support in the last three months were clearly less satisfied than the others. My director wants two things: to print the sentence 71 percent of our customers are satisfied in the annual report, and to cut the support team's budget, because contact with support seems to make people unhappy. I have the answers in a spreadsheet with the customer number, and I can get each customer's plan, region and tenure from the billing system. Nothing is exported yet. What should I tell him, and what would you do with the data?

I read the case file and noted the situation; here's my view before you touch the spreadsheet.

Customers with a recent problem (an outage, a billing error, a slow install) are exactly the ones who both contacted support and felt strongly enough to reply. So 71% is likely the optimistic end, not the middle. Printing "71% of our customers are satisfied" claims a result the survey wasn't designed to give.

**Why the budget cut follows the arrow backwards.** Support contact tracks low satisfaction largely because dissatisfied customers contact support — the contact is where the problem surfaces, not what creates it. And the people who contact support are still trying. Cut the team and you don't remove the problems; you raise the effort needed to report one, which converts "problem → fixed → stays" into "problem → unresolved → leaves". You'd be buying a saving today out of next year's churn.

**What I'd do with the data.**

1. Join the survey answers (customer number, date, score, support-contact flag and reason if you have it) to plan, region, tenure. Check how many of the 4,900 match a billing record.
2. Compare respondents with non-respondents on plan, region and tenure mix — that tells us how far the number can travel.
3. Re-measure the support gap *within* like-for-like groups (same plan, same tenure band, same region), since new customers contact more and score lower anyway.

Two things I'd still need from you: whether the export can carry the *reason* for the support contact, and what your annual report allows as wording.

Three ways to go from here, and my recommendation is the middle one first, because that is what your director actually needs in his hand.

I can write that now from what you've told me, and tighten it once we have numbers.

transcript.text: The survey read-out, done properly

Good pick — that's the one that actually arms you for both conversations. Here's how I'd run it, and the one thing I need from you first.

**The read-out, in four moves**

1. **Respondents vs non-respondents.** With a row for every customer and a "answered yes/no" flag, I compare the two groups on plan, region and tenure. If the 4,900 differ in mix — say they skew to long-tenure or premium customers — then 71% describes your *responders*, not your base, and we can say by how much.
2. **The support gap, adjusted.** Re-measure satisfied-vs-not among customers who contacted support against those who didn't, *within* the same plan, region and tenure band. New customers and troubled lines contact more and score lower on their own; the raw gap probably shrinks.
3. **A base-wide estimate.** Weight the responses back to the 80,000 by those mix differences, so you can quote a range rather than a single optimistic figure.
